title: 論語 八佾第三
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 3, 〈八佾〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 3 of the Analects, 八佾 Bā yì, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Eight rows (of dancers)…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Almost the whole book is about the rites and music: it opens with Confucius' anger at the great families of Lu who used the king's dances and hymns in their own halls (3.1–3.2), and goes on to what the rites are rooted in (3.3–3.4), sacrifice and the spirits (3.10–3.13), the Zhou dynasty's rites as the model (3.14), archery as a contest of gentlemen (3.7, 3.16), the minister Guan Zhong, great but no master of the rites (3.22), and music — how a performance unfolds (3.23) and the difference between music that is beautiful and music that is also good (3.25). Each numbered passage (3.1–3.26, the standard numbering) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 3.9 the edition we follow misprints 把 for 杞, the state of Qi; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
孔子謂季氏：「
八佾舞於庭，
是可忍也，
孰不可忍也？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Ji — the Jisun house of Lu
to bear to do, bring oneself to

sentences.i: Confucius said of the head of the Ji house: “He has eight rows of dancers performing in his courtyard. If he can bring himself to do this, there is nothing he will stop at.”
sentences.n: The book takes its name from 八佾 'eight rows' in its first line; Zhu Xi notes that all its 26 passages, with the last two of Book 2, concern the rites and music. 季氏 is the Jisun 季孫 house, the strongest of the three great families of Lu; He Yan's commentator Ma Rong names its head as Ji Huanzi. 佾 yì is a row of dancers. Zhu Xi: the Son of Heaven had eight rows, a feudal lord six, a grandee four, an officer two, each row with as many dancers as there were rows (so 8 × 8 = 64); he also records the view that every row had eight, which is He Yan's Ma Rong's, and says he cannot tell which is right. A grandee using the king's dance is a usurpation. 謂 here is 'to speak of (someone)', not 'to call'. The last line turns on 忍 'to bear': Zhu Xi takes it as 'to bring oneself to do' — if he can do this, what can he not do? — and records the other sense, 'to tolerate': if this can be tolerated, what cannot? He Yan's Ma Rong glosses 孰 as 誰 'who'. Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: the numbers step down by twos, and not a hair's breadth of usurpation is allowed between them.

sentences.t:
三家者以《雍》徹。
子曰：「『相維辟公，
天子穆穆』，
奚取於三家之堂？」

morph.gloss: the Yong — an ode of the Zhou royal temple
assisting, attending — Zhu Xi: 助也
the Son of Heaven — the Zhou king
solemn and grave, deep and still

sentences.l:
The Three Families cleared away to the Yong.
The Master said: “‘The helpers are the princes and dukes;
the Son of Heaven, solemn and still’ —
what of this is taken up in the halls of the Three Families?”
sentences.i: The Three Families had the Yong sung as the sacrificial vessels were cleared away. The Master said: “‘The princes and dukes attend him; the Son of Heaven stands solemn and grave’ — what in these words has any place in the halls of the Three Families?”
sentences.n: 三家 are the three great families of Lu, Mengsun, Shusun and Jisun; 者 after them marks the topic. 雍 is the ode 雝 in the Zhou temple hymns (Odes 282), sung when the vessels were cleared after the king's ancestral sacrifice; 徹 chè is 'to clear away'. The Master answers by quoting two of its lines. 相 is read xiàng, 'to assist' (Zhu Xi: 相去聲…助也), not xiāng 'mutually'. 維 is a copula particle common in the Odes, 'are'. 辟 is bì, 'lord, prince': Zhu Xi takes 辟公 as the feudal lords; He Yan's Bao Xian says the lords and the heirs of the two earlier royal houses, who came to help at the king's sacrifice. 穆穆 is the doubled adjective of the king's bearing, 'deep and remote'. 奚取 'what is taken?': in a grandee's hall there are no assisting princes and no Son of Heaven, so the words mean nothing there — Zhu Xi says the Master mocks their ignorant presumption. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: Lu itself was wrongly granted the king's rites and music for the Duke of Zhou's merit, and the families copied their own lord.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
人而不仁，
如禮何？
人而不仁，
如樂何？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A man, and yet not humane —
what of the rites?
A man, and yet not humane —
what of music?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man lacks humaneness, the rites will not answer to him. If a man lacks humaneness, music will not answer to him.”
sentences.n: 人而不仁: 而 between subject and predicate again gives 'a man, and yet not humane' (as 2.22 人而無信). 如…何 wraps round its object: 如禮何 'what about the rites, what can be done with them?' 樂 is yuè 'music' here. Zhu Xi quotes You Zuo: if a man is not humane his human heart is lost, and though he wants to use rites and music, they will not serve him. He also quotes Master Cheng — humaneness is the right order of the world; lose it and there is neither order nor ease — and a Mr Li, who suspects the editors set the saying here, after 3.1 and 3.2, because it was aimed at the families usurping the rites and music.

sentences.t: 林放問禮之本。

morph.gloss: Lin Fang — a man of Lu

sentences.l: Lin Fang asked about the root of the rites.
sentences.i: Lin Fang asked what lies at the root of the rites.
sentences.n: 林放 Lin Fang is known only from this book; Zhu Xi (and Zheng Xuan, in He Yan) say he was a man of Lu. Zhu Xi: he saw that those who practised the rites busied themselves with elaborate forms, and suspected the root was not there. 本 'root' is the word of 1.2, 'the gentleman works at the root'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
大哉問！
sentences.l: The Master said: “Great — the question!
sentences.i: The Master said: “That is a large question!
sentences.n: 大哉問 is an exclamation turned round: the predicate 大 'great' with 哉 comes first and the subject 問 'the question' last — 'great indeed, (this) question'. Zhu Xi: the age was chasing the branches, and Lin Fang alone cared about the root, so the Master made much of his question — get the root, and the whole body of the rites is in it.

sentences.t:
禮，與其奢也，寧儉；
喪，與其易也，寧戚。」
sentences.l:
With the rites, rather than lavish,
better sparing;
with mourning, rather than smoothly ordered,
better grieving.”
sentences.i: With the rites, too plain is better than too lavish. With mourning, real grief is better than forms gone through with ease.”
sentences.n: 與其…寧… 'rather than…, better…' is a pattern to learn: 與 is yǔ, and 其 'its' makes what follows a description of the thing. 喪 is sāng, 'mourning', the rites for the dead. 易 is yì: Zhu Xi glosses it 治 'well ordered' (he cites Mencius, 易其田疇 'to put one's fields in order') — in mourning, forms practised to fluency with no real grief behind them; He Yan's Bao Xian has 和易 'easy, at ease'. 戚 is grief. Zhu Xi: the rites prize the mean, and neither side of either pair hits it — the lavish and the smoothly ordered overshoot into ornament, the sparing and the grieving fall short into plainness — but the plain is nearer the root, since in all things substance comes before ornament. He quotes Fan Zuyu: better too little ceremony and enough reverence than the reverse; and Yang Shi: the rites began with food and drink, a hollow in the ground for a wine-jar and the hands cupped to drink — the vessels came later to adorn it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
夷狄之有君，
不如諸夏之亡也。」

morph.gloss: the Yi and the Di — the peoples of the east and north
the Xia states — the Chinese states

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The Yi and Di having rulers
is not like the Xia states lacking them.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Even the tribes of the east and north have their rulers — unlike the states of the Xia, which have none.”
sentences.n: 夷 and 狄 are the peoples outside the Zhou world to the east and north; 諸夏 'the many Xia' are the Chinese states. 之 between subject and verb makes each clause a noun phrase: 'the Yi-Di's having rulers', 'the Xia's lacking (them)'. 亡 is read wú and means 無 'not to have' — Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Wu that the two were used for each other in antiquity. The line can be taken two ways. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: even the barbarians have rulers and leaders, unlike the Xia states, where usurpation has wiped out the line between high and low; and he quotes Yin Tun that it is a lament for the times — not that the states had no rulers, but that their rulers could not rule. The other way of taking it: 'the barbarians, even with rulers, are not equal to the Xia states without them'.

sentences.t:
季氏旅於泰山。
子謂冉有曰：「女弗能救與？」
對曰：「不能。」
子曰：「嗚呼！
曾謂泰山不如林放乎？」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)
made the lü sacrifice — to a mountain
Ran You — the disciple Ran Qiu
You (from his courtesy name 子有)

sentences.l:
The Ji made the lü sacrifice to Mount Tai.
The Master spoke to Ran You, saying: “Can you not save him from it?”
He answered, saying: “I cannot.”
The Master said: “Alas!
Can it be said that Mount Tai is not the equal of Lin Fang?”
sentences.i: The head of the Ji house sacrificed to Mount Tai. The Master said to Ran You: “Can you not stop him?” “I cannot,” he replied. The Master said: “Alas! Are we to think Mount Tai knows less than Lin Fang?”
sentences.n: 冉有 Ran You is Ran Qiu 冉求 (courtesy name Ziyou 子有, not the Ziyou 子游 of 2.7), a disciple who served as steward 宰 of the Ji house. 旅 is the name of a sacrifice to mountains. By the rites, Zhu Xi says, a feudal lord sacrifices to the mountains and rivers within his borders; a grandee doing so usurps his lord's place. 女 is read rǔ, 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝); 與 at the end is yú, a question particle (與平聲). 弗 is a strong 'not', usually before a verb whose object is understood. 救 Zhu Xi takes as 'to save him from falling into the crime of usurpation'; He Yan's Ma Rong: 'to stop'. He Yan's text reads 不 for 弗, with no change of sense. 嗚呼 is a sigh, 'alas'. 曾 here is zēng, 'can it really be that…'. The god of the mountain, Zhu Xi explains, does not accept an offering against the rites; the Master hopes the Ji will see the sacrifice is useless and stop of his own accord, and holds up Lin Fang of 3.4, who asked for the root of the rites, to spur Ran You. He Yan's Bao Xian spells it out: Lin Fang at least knew the rites — is the god of Mount Tai to know less? He quotes Fan Zuyu: the Master knew Ran You could not be told, but a sage does not lightly give up on anyone.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子無所争，
必也射乎！
揖讓而升，
下而飲，
其争也君子。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman has nothing he contends over —
if he must, it would be archery!
Bowing and yielding he goes up;
coming down, (the loser) is made to drink:
his contending is a gentleman's.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman does not compete — unless it is at archery. Even there he bows and gives way as he goes up to the hall, and when they come down the loser drinks the forfeit cup. That is competing as a gentleman competes.”
sentences.n: 無所争 'has nothing that he contends over': 所 makes 争 'to contend' (the edition's form of 爭) into 'that which he contends over'. 必也…乎 is 'if it must be (something), surely it is…'. Zhu Xi describes the great archery rite: the archers go up to the hall in pairs, bowing three times before they ascend; when they have shot, they bow and come down, wait for the rest, and then the winners bow and the losers go up, take the cup, and drink it standing. 飲 is marked 去聲 by Zhu Xi, yìn 'to give to drink', the causative: the winner has the loser drink, as He Yan's Ma Rong also says ('the higher score makes the lower drink'). 其争也君子 'his contending is gentlemanly': even his one contest is courteous and unhurried, unlike a small man's.

sentences.t:
子夏問曰：「『巧笑倩兮，
美目盻兮，
素以為絢兮。』
何謂也？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
clear in black and white (= 盼 pàn)

sentences.l:
Zixia asked, saying: “‘The winning smile, how it dimples!
The lovely eyes, how clear their black and white!
The white ground made into colour!’
What does it mean?”
sentences.i: Zixia asked: “‘Her winning smile and its dimples, her lovely eyes so clear in their black and white — the plain silk made bright with colours.’ What does this mean?”
sentences.n: Zixia quotes a song; 兮 xī is the Odes' breathing particle at the end of a line. He Yan's Ma Rong says the first two lines are in the ode 碩人 'The Tall Lady' (Odes 57) and the third is lost; Zhu Xi calls the whole a lost ode. 倩 qiàn is the charm of the cheeks and mouth (Zhu Xi: 好口輔); 盻 is printed so in this edition but Zhu Xi reads it pàn (普莧反), the word written 盼, 'eyes with the black and white clearly marked' — not xì 'to glare'. 素 is the white ground laid for a painting, 絢 the coloured design. Zhu Xi: the lines say a woman already lovely in herself is adorned besides, as colours go on a white ground; Zixia suspected the reverse — that the plainness itself was the adornment — and so he asked. 何謂也 'what is meant?' as in 2.5.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
繪事後素。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “The work of painting comes after the white ground.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The painting comes after the white ground is laid.”
sentences.n: 繪事 'the business of painting'; 後 is a verb, 'to come after', and 後素 'after the white'. Zhu Xi cites the Kaogongji 考工記 (the craftsmen's chapter of the Zhou rites) for the same words: first a ground of white powder is laid as the base, then the five colours go on — as a person must have good substance before ornament can be added. He Yan keeps an older reading by Zheng Xuan that runs the other way: the colours are laid first, and white is put in last between them to set off the design — the white, like the rites, is what completes the beauty.

sentences.t:
曰：「禮後乎？」
子曰：「
起予者商也！
始可與言詩已矣。」

morph.gloss: the one who stirs up, brings out
at last, now for the first time

sentences.l:
He said: “The rites come after?”
The Master said: “The one who stirs me up is Shang!
Now at last one can talk the Odes with him.”
sentences.i: Zixia said: “Then the rites come afterwards?” The Master said: “Shang, you have woken my own thought. With you, at last, the Odes can be talked over.”
sentences.n: Zixia's leap: if colour comes after the white ground, the rites come after something more basic. Zhu Xi names it — the rites need wholeheartedness and good faith as their ground, as painting needs the white. 起予者商也 'the one who raises me is Shang': 予 yú is 'I, me', and 商 Shang is Zixia's personal name (Bu Shang 卜商), used by the Master as he uses Ci for Zigong. 起 Zhu Xi glosses 發 'to bring out' — Zixia has drawn out the Master's own thought. 始可與言詩已矣 repeats what was said to Zigong in 1.15. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: Zigong came to the Odes from talk about learning, Zixia to learning from talk about the Odes; and Yang Shi: 'the sweet takes seasoning, the white takes colour' — without the substance the rites have nothing to work on.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
夏禮，吾能言之，
杞不足徵也；
殷禮，吾能言之，
宋不足徵也。
文獻不足故也。
足，則吾能徵之矣。」

morph.gloss: Qi — the state of the Xia heirs
Song — the state of the Yin heirs

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The rites of Xia, I can speak of them,
but Qi does not suffice to bear them out;
the rites of Yin, I can speak of them,
but Song does not suffice to bear them out.
Records and worthies are not sufficient — that is the reason.
Were they sufficient, I could bear them out.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I can talk about the rites of the Xia, but its heirs in Qi have too little left to confirm what I say; I can talk about the rites of the Yin, but its heirs in Song have too little left to confirm it. There are not enough documents, and not enough men who know. If there were, I could prove my words.”
sentences.n: The print has 把, a misprint for 杞, corrected here. (Zhu Xi's comment has the same slip, 把夏之後; Ruan Yuan's reprint and He Yan's text both read 杞.) 杞 Qǐ — not the state of Qi 齊 — was the small state where the heirs of the Xia kept their ancestral sacrifices, as 宋 Song was for the heirs of the Yin (Shang). 徵 zhēng is 'to give evidence for' (Zhu Xi: 證也); He Yan's Bao Xian glosses it 成 'to bring to completion'. 文 is written records (Zhu Xi: 典籍), 獻 the worthy men who remember (Zhu Xi: 賢也); later the two together became the word for 'documents'. 文獻不足故也 is a reason clause: '(it is) because records and worthies are insufficient'. 足則 'if sufficient, then'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
禘自既灌而往者，
吾不欲觀之矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The di sacrifice, from when the libation has been poured onward —
I have no wish to watch it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “At the great di sacrifice, once the libation has been poured, I have no wish to watch any more.”
sentences.n: 禘 dì is a great royal sacrifice. Zhu Xi quotes Zhao Kuang (Zhao Boxun): the king, having a temple to the founder of his line, also sacrifices there to the ancestor from whom the founder sprang, with the founder as companion. Zhu Xi adds that King Cheng granted Lu this rite for the Duke of Zhou's merit, but it was not proper for a feudal state. 灌 guàn is the pouring of fragrant millet wine on the ground at the start, to bring the spirits down. 自既灌而往 'from (when it is) already poured, onward'; 者 makes the whole a topic. Zhu Xi: until the libation the lord and ministers of Lu still had some sincerity; after it they grew slack, a fault on top of an improper rite. He Yan's Kong Anguo gives another cause: after the libation the ancestral tablets were set in order of generations, and Lu had raised Duke Xi above his elder predecessor, upsetting that order.

sentences.t:
或問禘之説。
子曰：「不知也。
知其説者之於天下也，
其如示諸斯乎！」
指其掌。
sentences.l:
Someone asked the meaning of the di.
The Master said: “I do not know.
One who knew its meaning, with regard to the world —
would it not be like looking at it here!”
He pointed to his palm.
sentences.i: Someone asked what the di sacrifice meant. The Master said: “I do not know. Whoever did know would see the whole world as plainly as this” — and he pointed to his palm.
sentences.n: 説 is the edition's form of 說, here shuō 'explanation, what it means'. Why 'I do not know'? Zhu Xi: the di expressed, more deeply than any rite, the gratitude that goes back to the source, and was beyond the questioner; and the rule 'one who is not king does not perform the di' was something Lu had to keep quiet about. He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same more briefly: the answer spared the lord of Lu. 示 Zhu Xi reads as 視 'to look at' (示與視同); He Yan's Bao Xian keeps 'to show', as one points out a thing lying in the palm. 諸 is the fused 之於 'it in' and 斯 'this', the palm. Whoever understood the di, Zhu Xi says, would find nothing unclear in principle, and governing the world would not be hard. The last line, 指其掌, is the disciples' note of the gesture.

sentences.t:
祭如在，
祭神如神在。
sentences.l:
Sacrificing, as though present;
sacrificing to the spirits, as though the spirits present.
sentences.i: When he made offerings to his forebears, it was as though they stood before him; when he made offerings to the spirits, it was as though the spirits stood before him.
sentences.n: There is no 子曰: this is the disciples' record of how the Master sacrificed (Zhu Xi: 門人記孔子祭祀之誠意). 在 is 'to be present, to be there'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: the first 祭 is the sacrifice to one's ancestors, 祭神 to spirits outside the family; the first rests on filial devotion, the second on reverence. He Yan's Kong Anguo has 'serve the dead as one serves the living', and takes the spirits as the hundred gods.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾不與祭，
如不祭。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “If I do not take part in the sacrifice,
it is as if I did not sacrifice.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If I am not there in person at a sacrifice, it is as though no sacrifice were made.”
sentences.n: 與 is read yù here, 'to take part in' (Zhu Xi: 與去聲), not yǔ 'with'. The saying explains the line before. Zhu Xi: if he was kept away and had someone stand in for him, the sincerity of 'as if present' could not be given, and though the sacrifice was made, his heart felt it as never made. He quotes Fan Zuyu: the gentleman fasts and purifies himself for days before a sacrifice, until he sees the one he sacrifices to; where the sincerity is, the spirit is.

sentences.t:
王孫賈問曰：「『與其媚於奥，
寧媚於竈』，
何謂也？」

morph.gloss: Wangsun Jia — a grandee of Wei
the south-west corner — the place of honour

sentences.l:
Wangsun Jia asked, saying: “‘Rather than court the corner of honour,
better court the stove’ —
what does it mean?”
sentences.i: Wangsun Jia asked: “What do they mean when they say, ‘Better to get on the right side of the stove than of the place of honour in the corner’?”
sentences.n: 王孫賈 Wangsun Jia was a grandee of Wei 衞 and, Zhu Xi says, the real power there. He quotes a saying. 媚 is to court someone's favour (Zhu Xi: 親順 'to draw close and comply'). 奥 (the edition's form of 奧 ào) is the south-west corner of a room, the place of honour; 竈 zào is the stove, whose god received one of the five household sacrifices, in summer. Zhu Xi: in the household rites the offering was first set at the stove and then the impersonator of the dead was received in the corner, so the corner had constant honour but was not where the business was done, while the lowly stove was where things happened. The saying meant: better to attach yourself to the minister in power than to the lord — and Jia, being that minister, was hinting to Confucius. He Yan's Kong Anguo reads the corner as the lord's intimates and the stove as the man who holds the government.

sentences.t:
子曰：「不然。
獲罪於天，
無所禱也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not so.
One who has incurred guilt against Heaven
has nothing to pray to.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Not so. Once you stand guilty before Heaven, no prayer will help you.”
sentences.n: 不然 'not so' refuses the saying. 獲罪 is 'to get guilt', to offend. 無所禱 'there is nothing to which to pray': 所 again makes 'that which (one prays to)'. Zhu Xi: Heaven is principle itself, 天即理也, honoured beyond comparison with corner or stove; go against principle and you offend Heaven, and no courting of corner or stove will buy you off — so one should court neither, only follow principle. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: the sage's words are modest and not pressing; if Jia understood them they would do him good, and if he did not, they would still bring no harm on the speaker. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes Heaven as a figure for the lord.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
周監於二代，
郁郁乎文哉！
吾從周。」

morph.gloss: rich in pattern, flourishing (Zhu Xi: 郁郁文盛貌)
rich in pattern, flourishing (Zhu Xi: 郁郁文盛貌)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The Zhou looked to the two dynasties —
how richly patterned!
I follow the Zhou.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The Zhou could look back on the two dynasties before it, and how richly patterned its forms became! I go with the Zhou.”
sentences.n: 監 is jiàn, 'to look at, to look to' (Zhu Xi: 監視也); the two dynasties are the Xia and the Shang (Yin). Zhu Xi: the Zhou looked at their rites and took from and added to them, as in 2.23. 郁郁 yù yù is a doubled adjective, 'flourishing, rich' (Zhu Xi: 文盛貌 'the look of abundant pattern'); with 乎 and 哉 the predicate comes first, as in 大哉問. 文 is pattern, the whole ordered form of the rites and institutions. 從 is cóng 'to follow'. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: by the Zhou the rites of the three dynasties were complete, and the Master admired their pattern and followed it.

sentences.t:
子入大廟，
每事問。
或曰：「孰謂鄹人之子知禮乎？
入大廟，
每事問。」
子聞之，曰：「是禮也。」

morph.gloss: the Grand Temple — of the Duke of Zhou, in Lu

sentences.l:
The Master entered the Grand Temple;
about each thing he asked.
Someone said: “Who says the son of the man from Zou knows the rites?
He enters the Grand Temple —
about each thing he asks.”
The Master heard of it and said: “This is the rite.”
sentences.i: When the Master went into the Grand Temple, he asked about every detail. Someone said: “Who says that fellow from Zou knows the rites? In the Grand Temple he asks about everything.” Hearing of it, the Master said: “To ask like that is what the rites require.”
sentences.n: 大廟 is read tàimiào (Zhu Xi: 大音泰), the Grand Temple: in Lu, the temple of the Duke of Zhou. Zhu Xi suggests this was when Confucius first held office and went in to assist at a sacrifice. 鄹 Zōu was a town of Lu where his father, Shuliang He 叔梁紇, had been the officer; 鄹人之子 'the son of the Zou man' is a slighting way to name him. 每事問 puts the object first: 'each thing (he) asked'. 孰謂…乎 'who says…?' Zhu Xi: Confucius was known from youth for knowing the rites, so the speaker used this to sneer; but care and reverence carried to the full is itself the rite. He quotes Yin Tun: the rites are reverence; even knowing, to ask is the height of care.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
射不主皮，
為力不同科，
古之道也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “In archery, not making (piercing) the hide the main thing,
because strength is not of one grade —
that was the way of antiquity.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “In archery the point is to hit the leather, not to drive through it, for men are not all given the same strength. That was how the ancients did it.”
sentences.n: 皮 is hide: Zhu Xi explains that a cloth target was hung with a piece of leather at its centre, the bull's-eye. 射不主皮 is a line of the village archery rite (鄉射禮) — the aim is to hit, not to pierce; 為力不同科 is the Master's explanation, with 為 read wèi 'because' (Zhu Xi: 為去聲), and 科 kē 'grade, rank'. Archery in antiquity was a way of observing virtue, Zhu Xi says, and strength differs from man to man; when Zhou rites declined and the states were at war, they went back to valuing the shot that pierces armour, and the Master lamented it. He quotes Yang Shi: accuracy can be learned, strength cannot be forced. He Yan's Ma Rong reads the two halves apart: 為力 'labour service', which was divided into three grades.

sentences.t: 子貢欲去告朔之餼羊。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
announcing the new moon — a monthly rite
new moon, first day of the month

sentences.l: Zigong wanted to do away with the live sheep of the new-moon announcement.
sentences.i: Zigong wanted to stop the offering of a live sheep at the announcement of the new moon.
sentences.n: 告朔 is read gùshuò (Zhu Xi: 告古篤反), 'announcing the new moon'. Zhu Xi explains the rite: each winter the Son of Heaven issued the calendar for the coming year to the feudal lords, who kept it in their ancestral temple, and on the first of each month a lord announced the month there with a sheep and put its calendar into effect. 餼 xì is a live sacrificial animal (Zhu Xi: 生牲). From Duke Wen's time the lords of Lu had stopped attending the rite, but the officials still supplied the sheep — so Zigong wanted to drop it. 去 is 'to remove'; Zhu Xi marks the old rising-tone reading for this verb (起吕反, qǔ), which modern practice does not keep: we give qù.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
賜也！
爾愛其羊，
我愛其禮。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Ci, you mind losing the sheep; I mind losing the rite.”
sentences.n: 賜 Ci is Zigong's personal name, as in 1.15; 也 after a name in address is a calling pause. 爾 ěr is 'you' (He Yan's text writes 汝 rǔ, the same word for our purpose). 愛 here is not 'love' but 'to grudge, to be loath to lose' (Zhu Xi: 愛猶惜也): Zigong grudged the waste on a rite that was no longer real. But while the sheep remained, Zhu Xi says, the rite could still be recognized and one day restored; take the sheep away too and the rite would be gone. He quotes Yang Shi: so long as the sheep remains, the name of the rite has not died, and the substance can be revived.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
事君盡禮，
人以為諂也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Serving one's lord with the rites in full —
others take it for fawning.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Serve your lord with every courtesy the rites require, and people will call it fawning.”
sentences.n: 盡禮 'to exhaust the rites', to carry them out in full. 以為 'to take as' (2.8). Zhu Xi quotes a Mr Huang: Confucius added nothing to the rites of serving a lord, he only did them in full; the men of the day could not, and so called it fawning. He also quotes Master Cheng: another man would have said 'the small men call it fawning'; the sage said only 'others' — the breadth of his virtue shows even here. He Yan's text lacks the final 也.

sentences.t:
定公問：「
君使臣，臣事君，
如之何？」
孔子對曰：「
君使臣以禮，
臣事君以忠。」

morph.gloss: Duke Ding — the ruler of Lu
to be like, to come up to
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Duke Ding asked: “The lord employing his ministers,
the ministers serving the lord —
how should it be?”
Kongzi answered, saying:
“The lord employs his ministers by the rites;
the ministers serve the lord wholeheartedly.”
sentences.i: Duke Ding asked: “How should a lord employ his ministers, and how should ministers serve their lord?” Confucius replied: “A lord should employ his ministers as the rites require, and ministers should serve their lord with all their heart.”
sentences.n: 定公 is Duke Ding of Lu (r. 509–495 BC), under whom Confucius held office; Zhu Xi gives his personal name as Song 宋. As in 2.19, the book writes 孔子對曰 when the Master answers a ruler. 如之何 'how is it to be done?' (2.20). 臣 is a minister, any servant of the lord. Zhu Xi: both answers are what principle requires, and each side should give its utmost. He quotes Lü Dalin: a lord should not worry that his ministers are not wholehearted but that his own rites fall short; a minister should not worry that his lord lacks the rites but that his own wholeheartedness falls short; and Yin Tun: lord and minister are joined by what is right.

sentences.t:
子曰：「《關雎》，
樂而不淫，
哀而不傷。」

morph.gloss: the Guanju — the first of the Odes

sentences.i: The Master said: “The ‘Guanju’ has joy in it that never runs to excess, and sorrow that never turns to harm.”
sentences.n: 關雎 Guanju, named from its opening words 關關雎鳩 'guan guan cry the ospreys', is the first poem of the Odes. 樂 here is lè 'joy' (Zhu Xi: 樂音洛). 淫 is joy overflowing until it loses its rightness; 傷 is grief carried so far it harms one's ease (Zhu Xi). He reads the poem as about a queen whose virtue fits her to be a lord's mate: before she is found there is longing, tossing and turning at night; when she is found there is lute and drum — the longing deep but not harmful, the joy full but not wanton. He would have the learner savour the words and listen to the music, to know feelings in their right measure.

sentences.t:
哀公問社於宰我。
宰我對曰：「
夏后氏以松，
殷人以栢，
周人以栗，
曰：使民戰栗。」

morph.gloss: Zai Wo — the disciple Zai Yu
Wo (from his courtesy name 子我)
a steward, the chief officer of a noble house

sentences.l:
Duke Ai asked Zai Wo about the altar of the soil.
Zai Wo answered, saying: “The Xia royal house used the pine,
the men of Yin used the cypress,
the men of Zhou used the chestnut —
meaning: ‘make the people tremble.’”
sentences.i: Duke Ai asked Zai Wo about the altar of the soil. Zai Wo replied: “The Xia planted the pine, the Yin the cypress, and the Zhou the chestnut — meaning, to make the people quake.”
sentences.n: 宰我 Zai Wo is the disciple Zai Yu 宰予 (courtesy name Ziwo 子我), known for his ready tongue. 社 shè is the altar to the god of the soil that every state kept. Zhu Xi: each dynasty planted at it the tree best suited to its land, as the god's seat. 夏后氏 is 'the Xia sovereign house'. 栢 is the edition's form of 柏 bǎi 'cypress'. Zai Wo's last line is a pun: 栗 lì 'chestnut' is also the 栗 of 戰栗 'to shiver, to tremble with fear'. Zhu Xi wonders whether he was drawing on the old practice of executing men at the altar of the soil. He Yan's text ends the speech with 也; He Yan's Kong Anguo says Zai Wo did not know the real reason and made this one up.

sentences.t:
子聞之，曰：「
成事不說，
遂事不諫，
既往不咎。」
sentences.i: The Master heard of it and said: “What is done is done and not worth arguing; what is already in train cannot be talked back; what is past is past, and no use finding fault.”
sentences.n: 說 is shuō 'to speak of, to discuss' (He Yan's Bao Xian: 解說 'to explain'). Zhu Xi: 遂事 is a thing not yet finished but past stopping. 諫 is to remonstrate, to try to talk someone out of a course. 咎 is to blame. Zhu Xi: Zai Wo's answer missed the meaning of the altar and might stir the duke's taste for killing, but the words were out and could not be taken back; so the Master listed these three to rebuke him sharply and make him careful afterwards. He quotes Yin Tun: the ancients named each altar from the tree that grew well there, and drew no meaning from the tree.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
管仲之器小哉！」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Guan Zhong's capacity — small indeed!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Guan Zhong was a man of narrow capacity!”
sentences.n: 管仲 Guan Zhong (personal name Yiwu 夷吾) was chief minister to Duke Huan of Qi 齊 in the seventh century BC and made him leader of the feudal lords. 器 is a vessel, here what a man can hold, his measure (compare 2.12 'the gentleman is not a vessel'). Zhu Xi: he did not know the great learning of sages and worthies, so his scope was shallow and his plans low; he could not set himself right and bring his lord to the kingly Way.

sentences.t:
或曰：「管仲儉乎？」
曰：「管氏有三歸，
官事不攝，
焉得儉？」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
the Sangui — Zhu Xi: a terrace

sentences.l:
Someone said: “Was Guan Zhong frugal?”
He said: “The Guan house had the Sangui,
and its offices were not doubled up —
how could he be frugal?”
sentences.i: Someone said: “Was Guan Zhong frugal, then?” The Master said: “The Guan house had the Sangui, and no officer of his household ever held two posts. How could he be frugal?”
sentences.n: The questioner, Zhu Xi says, thought 'small capacity' meant 'frugal'. 管氏 'the Guan house' is the man and his household. 三歸 is disputed. Zhu Xi takes it as the name of a terrace, citing the Shuoyuan 說苑; He Yan's Bao Xian reads it 'married three wives of three surnames' (歸 is a woman's going to her husband's house). Either way it is extravagance. 攝 is to hold more than one post (Zhu Xi: 兼也): a grandee's household officers should each cover several tasks, but Guan Zhong had a full staff. 焉 is yān, 'how?' (Zhu Xi: 於䖍反). He Yan's text ends 焉得儉乎, with a final 乎.

sentences.t:
然則管仲知禮乎？」
曰：「
邦君樹塞門，管氏亦樹塞門；
邦君為兩君之好
有反坫，管氏亦有反坫。
管氏而知禮，
孰不知禮？」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
a cup-stand — for returning the cups
a mound of earth between the pillars of a hall for setting cups on (Zhu Xi: 坫在兩楹之閒)

sentences.l:
“Then did Guan Zhong know the rites?”
He said: “The rulers of states set up a screen at the gate;
the Guan house too set up a screen at the gate.
The rulers of states, holding a friendly meeting of two lords,
have a cup-stand;
the Guan house too had a cup-stand.
If the Guan house knew the rites,
who does not know the rites?”
sentences.i: “Then did Guan Zhong know the rites?” The Master said: “Rulers of states put up a screen inside their gates, and so did Guan. Rulers of states, when two lords meet in friendship, have a stand for the emptied cups, and so did Guan. If Guan knew the rites, who is there that doesn't?”
sentences.n: 然則 'that being so, then': the same questioner, Zhu Xi says, now took 'not frugal' to mean 'knowing the rites' (He Yan's text puts 曰 before 然則, marking the new question). 樹 is the screen (Zhu Xi: 屏謂之樹) and 塞 sè 'to block from view' (塞猶蔽也): a screen set inside the gate to shut off inner from outer. 為兩君之好 'holding a friendly meeting of two lords': 為 is wéi 'to hold, to conduct' (He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 與鄰國君為好會) and 好 is the friendly meeting; Zhu Xi marks it 去聲 (hào), modern practice reads hǎo. 反坫 is a stand of earth between the two pillars of the hall where, after the toasts, the cups were turned down again (坫 diàn; Zhu Xi: 反爵於其上). Both belonged to a ruler of a state; Guan Zhong, a grandee, used them. 管氏而知禮 'the Guan house, and yet knowing the rites': 而 between subject and predicate makes a supposition, 'if…'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: extravagant and offending the rites — that is how one knows his capacity was small; a large vessel would know the rites by itself.

sentences.t:
子語魯大師樂，曰：「樂其可知也：
始作，翕如也；
從之，純如也，
皦如也，
繹如也，以成。」
sentences.l:
The Master told the Grand Music-Master of Lu about music, saying:
“Music can surely be known:
at the start, striking up — all gathered together;
let loose — blended,
clear,
unbroken,
and so complete.”
sentences.i: The Master talked to the Grand Music-Master of Lu about music. He said: “What music is can be known. It starts with everything coming in together; then, let loose, it blends, each part rings clear, and it flows on without a break to the end.”
sentences.n: 語 is read yù, 'to tell, to instruct' (Zhu Xi: 語去聲…告也), not yǔ 'words'. 大師 is tàishī (Zhu Xi: 大音泰), the Grand Music-Master, chief musician of the court; Zhu Xi says music had decayed and the Master was teaching him. Both 樂 are yuè 'music'. 如 after a descriptive word makes it a manner-word, like English '-ly': 翕如 'in a gathered way'. Zhu Xi's glosses: 翕 'joined together', 從 read zòng (從音縱) 'let go, given free course', 純 'harmonious', 皦 'clear, distinct', 繹 'continuing without a break', 成 the close of a piece. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: the notes join; joined, they blend like the five flavours; blended, each must keep its place and not drown the others; yet they are not isolated but run on like pearls on a string. He Yan's text reads 樂其可知已也.

sentences.t:
儀封人請見，曰：「
君子之至於斯也，
吾未嘗不得見也。」
從者見之。
出曰：「
二三子何患於喪乎？
天下之無道也久矣，
天將以夫子為木鐸。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
you, my friends — addressing the disciples
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
a wooden-clappered bell — rung to proclaim orders

sentences.l:
The border warden of Yi asked to be presented, saying:
“When a gentleman comes to this place,
I have never failed to get to see him.”
The followers presented him.
Coming out, he said: “My friends, why worry about losing office?
The world has been without the Way a long time;
Heaven is about to take your master for its wooden-clappered bell.”
sentences.i: The border warden at Yi asked to be presented. “Whenever a gentleman has come this way,” he said, “I have always managed to see him.” The disciples took him in. When he came out he said: “My friends, why be troubled that he has lost his place? The world has gone without the Way for a long time now. Heaven means to make your Master the bell that calls it to order.”
sentences.n: 儀 Yi was a town of Wei, according to Zhu Xi; 封人 is the officer who kept the border. Zhu Xi guesses he was a worthy man hiding in a low post. Zhu Xi marks two 見 as xiàn, 'to be presented, to present' (請見, 見之: 賢遍反): he asked for an audience, and the disciples got him one. In 不得見 it is jiàn 'to see'. 君子 here, Zhu Xi says, means the worthy men of the day. 未嘗不 'never once not': a double negative, 'always'. 從者 'those following', the disciples travelling with the Master; Zhu Xi marks 從 去聲 (zòng) for 'attendant', modern practice reads cóng. 二三子 'you two or three' is the friendly way to address a group of disciples. 喪 is sàng 'to lose' (Zhu Xi: 去聲): he takes it as losing office and leaving one's state. 木鐸 is a metal bell with a wooden clapper (Zhu Xi: 金口木舌), shaken when government orders were proclaimed. Zhu Xi: the disorder had gone as far as it could, order must come, and Heaven would give the Master office to spread his teaching. He records another reading: as the bell is carried through the roads, Heaven made him lose office so he would travel the four quarters teaching. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 喪 differently: 'why worry that the Master's sage virtue will be lost?' He Yan's text has 斯者 for 斯也, and lacks the 也 after 無道.

sentences.t:
子謂《韶》：「盡美矣，又盡善也。」
謂《武》：「盡美矣，未盡善也。」

morph.gloss: the Shao — the music of Shun
the Wu — the music of King Wu

sentences.l:
The Master said of the Shao: “Wholly beautiful, and wholly good as well.”
Of the Wu he said: “Wholly beautiful, but not yet wholly good.”
sentences.i: Of the Shao music the Master said: “It is as beautiful as music can be, and as good, too.” Of the Wu: “As beautiful as music can be, but not altogether good.”
sentences.n: 韶 Shao is the music of the sage king Shun, 武 Wu that of King Wu, founder of the Zhou. 盡 jìn is 'to the utmost, wholly'. Zhu Xi: 美 is the splendour of the sound and the dance, 善 the reality behind the beauty. Shun succeeded Yao and King Wu overthrew the tyrant Zhou of Shang to save the people — the achievement was one, so both musics are wholly beautiful. But Shun's virtue was his by nature and he received the world by Yao's yielding it to him; King Wu's virtue was regained by effort and he took the world by war; so their reality was not the same. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: Tang, who banished the last Xia king, felt shame, and so did King Wu — not their wish, but what their times demanded.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
居上不寛，
為禮不敬，
臨喪不哀，
吾何以觀之哉？」
sentences.i: The Master said: “High place without generosity, the rites without reverence, a funeral without grief — what is left in such a man for me to look at?”
sentences.n: 寛 is the edition's form of 寬 kuān 'broad, generous'. 喪 is sāng 'mourning' (as in 3.4). Each clause names a role and the thing at its root: Zhu Xi says generosity is the root of holding high place, since its business is to love men; reverence is the root of the rites, grief of mourning. Without the root, by what would one judge whether what a man does succeeds or fails? 何以 'by what', with the question word put before 以 as in 2.7.
